title: How B2B Support Software Is Priced: A Practical Guide | Pylon
summary: Per seat, per resolution, or usage credits? A practical guide to how B2B customer support software is priced, what drives the bill, and what to ask before you sign.
body_markdown:
> **The short version:** Most B2B support software charges in one of three ways: per seat, per resolution, or by usage credits. Many tools mix them. The sticker price per seat is only part of the bill. What really moves your cost is how AI is billed, which features sit on higher plans, and what add-ons you need. Before you sign, model your cost at today's ticket volume and at twice that volume.


Picture the budget meeting. Someone shares a pricing page. It says a number per seat, per month. Everyone nods.


Then the contract shows up. There's an AI line item. There's a platform add-on. Slack support is on a higher plan. The number on the pricing page was real, it just wasn't the whole bill.


This happens a lot. Not because anyone is hiding anything, but because support pricing has gotten more complicated as AI got added. Here's how it works.


## The three ways support software is priced


### 1. Per seat


This is the classic model. You pay a set amount for each person who works tickets, usually per month, often billed on an annual contract.


It's easy to understand and easy to budget. Your cost grows when your team grows, not when your customers send more tickets.


A few things to check:


- **Who counts as a seat?** Usually anyone who replies to tickets. Some tools also let people view tickets without a full seat.
- **Is there a minimum?** Many B2B tools have a minimum seat count.
- **Annual vs monthly.** The price you see is often the annual rate. Monthly billing can cost more.


### 2. Per resolution (or per ticket)


This model is newer and mostly tied to AI. You pay each time an AI agent resolves a conversation, or for each ticket or conversation handled.


The pitch is simple: you only pay when it works. And for a team with low volume, it can be cheap to start.


The catch is that your bill now grows with your ticket volume. A product launch, an outage, or a big new customer can spike your cost in a month you didn't plan for.


**What counts as "resolved"?**


This one trips up a lot of teams. Every vendor defines a resolution a little differently. Depending on the tool, a conversation might count as resolved when:


- The AI answers and the conversation auto-closes
- The customer says thanks or clicks "that helped"
- An agent marks it done
- The customer doesn't reply for a set number of days
- The customer doesn't come back about the same issue within a set window


Those aren't the same thing. A tool that counts "no reply in 24 hours" as resolved will report more resolutions, and bill you for more, than one that waits for the customer to confirm the problem is fixed.


So a lower price per resolution isn't always cheaper. Before you compare, ask each vendor exactly how they define a resolution. Then line up the numbers on the same definition.


### 3. Usage credits


Here you buy a pool of credits, and AI features draw from it. A simple automated answer might use a few credits. A deep investigation that checks logs, past tickets, and your codebase uses more.


Credits let you spend AI budget where it helps most, instead of paying the same price for every ticket. Most tools sell credits in committed packages for a year, with a way to top up if you run out.


The thing to check is how clearly the tool shows what each action costs, and whether you can see usage as it happens.


## Most tools mix these models


In practice, few tools use just one model. A common setup looks like this:


- **Seats** for the people who work tickets
- **AI on top** , billed per resolution, per seat, or with credits
- **Add-ons** for things like phone support, account health tools, or extra security
- **Plan tiers** that unlock features like a customer portal, custom reporting, or SSO


That's why two tools with the same seat price can end up with very different bills.


## What actually drives your bill


When you compare tools, these are the things that move the number the most.


- **How AI is billed.** This is now the biggest variable. Per resolution grows with volume, and with how loosely the vendor defines a resolution. Credits grow with how much work the AI does. A flat AI add-on per seat grows with team size.
- **Which channels are on which plan.** If your customers live in Slack or Microsoft Teams, check that those channels are on the plan you're pricing, not just the top one.
- **Plan tiers.** Features like a customer portal, custom reports, data warehouse sync, and SSO often sit on higher plans.
- **Add-ons.** Phone, account intelligence, and security features are often priced separately.
- **Contract terms.** Annual contracts, multi-year deals, and upfront commitments usually come with better rates.
- **Seat minimums.** A low per-seat price with a high minimum can cost more than it looks.


## How to estimate your real cost


Here's a simple way to build a number you can trust.


1. **Count your seats.** List everyone who works tickets. Then list people who only need to see them.
2. **Pick the plan you actually need.** Check that your channels and must-have features are on it.
3. **Estimate your AI usage.** Look at last month's tickets. How many are simple? How many need real digging? Ask the vendor to turn that into a cost.
4. **Add the add-ons.** Phone, account health, SSO, anything else you'll need in year one.
5. **Run it again at twice the tickets.** This is the most important step. A pricing model that looks cheap today can look very different when volume doubles.


If a vendor can't help you do this math, that's a signal.


## Questions to ask before you sign


- What's the total price for my team, with the AI I'll actually use?
- How does my bill change if ticket volume doubles?
- What counts as a seat? Do you have view-only seats?
- Which plan includes Slack, Teams, and my other channels?
- How is AI usage measured, and can I see it in real time?
- How do you define a resolution? Does the customer have to confirm, or does no reply count?
- What happens if I run out of AI budget mid-year?
- Is there a discount for committing upfront or signing for more than a year?


For a broader checklist that goes beyond price, see[how to evaluate an agentic support platform](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/how-to-evaluate-agentic-support-platforms) .


## Why B2B teams should care about per-ticket pricing


B2B support is different. You have fewer customers, but each one is worth a lot and their questions are harder. One account can have dozens of people asking questions in a shared Slack channel.


That means ticket volume can jump fast as you grow, especially if you run support in Slack. We cover that in[Slack-first support for B2B teams](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/slack-first-b2b-support) .


If your price is tied to every ticket, growth gets expensive in a new way. That's why a lot of B2B teams look for pricing that stays predictable as volume climbs. We go deeper on how to scale without the bill or the headcount running away in[how B2B support teams scale without just hiring](https://www.usepylon.com/blog/scale-b2b-support-without-hiring) .

## FAQ


### How much does B2B customer support software cost?


It depends on the pricing model, your team size, and how much AI you use. Most tools charge per seat per month, then add AI usage, plan tiers, and add-ons on top. To get a real number, count your seats, pick the plan that includes your channels, estimate AI usage from last month's tickets, and add any add-ons.


### What's the difference between per-seat and per-resolution pricing?


Per-seat pricing charges for each person who works tickets, so cost grows with your team. Per-resolution pricing charges each time an AI agent resolves a conversation, so cost grows with your ticket volume. Vendors define "resolved" differently, so check the definition before you compare prices. Many tools combine both.


### What are AI credits in support software?


Credits are a prepaid pool that AI features draw from. Simple actions use fewer credits and deep investigations use more. They let you spend AI budget on the work that matters instead of paying the same price per ticket.


### Is per-ticket pricing a good fit for B2B support?


It can be hard to budget. B2B ticket volume can jump quickly, especially with shared Slack channels, and per-ticket pricing makes your bill grow with every ticket. Many B2B teams prefer pricing that stays predictable as volume grows.
